sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Yurlungur** ​(*yurlungur*) — ‌Copper Snake, ‌Initiator ​· The ​great copper ​snake — ​belongs ​to the ‌Aboriginal tradition, ​where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the ‌domain "Copper ​Snake, Initiator". ‌The ​name means ​"The great ​copper snake"[^1].

​**Yurlungur** ​is the ‌great copper ​python ‌of the ​Yolŋu peoples ‌of ​northeast Arnhem ‌Land — ​a ‌Rainbow Serpent ​whose swallowing ​of the ‌boy ‌Wawi at ‌the first ​circumcision ​became the ‌template for ​male ​initiation across ‌the Murngin ​world. ​He is ‌not merely ​a monster; ‌he ​is the ​law itself, ​the ​waterhole guardian, ‌and the ‌ancestor ​who transforms ‌boys into ​men.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Yurlungur** ‌and ‌serves its ​temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/yurlungur/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— a ​description computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *yurlungur* ‌survives as ​a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the ​early domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; **Yurlungur** ​is ​a scholarly ​transliteration ‌of the ​reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"The ‌great copper ​snake"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form ​*yurlungur* survives ​only ‌because the ​early ‌domain-name system ​could ‌not carry ​diacritics; ‌it is ​a ‌technological compromise, ​not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ‌The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Yurlungur** ​recovers the ‌full ​diacritic detail ​of ‌the scholarly ​transliteration ​directly in ‌the ​address bar. ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— a ​description ‌computed from ‌the ​displayed form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ‌**y** → ‌**Y** ‌— Same, ​capitalized

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈjʊəlʊŋɡʊə/** ‌— Yolŋu/Murngin reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by phoneme:

- ​**Yur-** — Initial ​syllable with postalveolar ​approximant [j] and ​central vowel [ʊə] ‌— the name ​opens with the ​same glide heard ‌in English 'yes' ​followed by a ‌soft, rounded r-coloured ​vowel.
- **-lun-** ‌— Alveolar lateral ​[l] plus open-mid ​back vowel [ʊ] ​and alveolar nasal ​[n]; the middle ​syllable is level ‌and unaccented in ​the Yolŋu song ‌register.
- **-gur** — ​Voiced velar stop ‌[ɡ] followed by ​central r-coloured vowel ‌[ʊə]; the final ​syllable carries the ‌weight of the ​word in English ​scholarly pronunciation.

For ‌the modern speaker, ‌the closest approximation ‌is: 'YUR-lun-gur' — ​three level syllables, ​with the first ‌syllable receiving a ​light stress. Keep ​the 'r' soft; ‌this is an ​anglicized scholarly rendering ​of a Yolŋu ‌name.

Kindred ​and historical forms ‌of the name:

- ​**Yolŋu Matha** — ​Yurluŋgur, the great ​copper python of ​northeast Arnhem Land, ‌written in modern ‌Yolŋu orthography
- **Alternative ​spellings** — Yulunggur, ‌Julunggul, Yurlungar — ​variants collected by ​Berndt and Warner ‌from different Murngin/Yolŋu ‌clan groups
- **English ‌gloss** — 'Great ‌copper snake' or ​'copper python', the ‌Rainbow Serpent of ​the Murngin initiation ​cult

The ideal ​form would preserve ‌Yolŋu retroflex or ​postalveolar phonemes, but ​these are not ​registrable in the ‌DNS root zone. ​PuniCodex therefore records ​the conventional English ​scholarly spelling ‌**Yurlungur** with initial ​capitalization. The name ‌keeps its restoration ​plain: the restoration ‌capitalizes the proper ​noun but does ‌not add a ‌diacritic or distinctive ​letter that the ​ASCII form lacks, ​because the Aboriginal ​source is transmitted ‌orally and is ‌conventionally romanized without ​special marks.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous writing ‌system ‌is securely ​attested ​for individual ​aboriginal ​names. The ​form ‌shown is ​a ​modern ‌scholarly transliteration.[^1]

​The ‌form **Yurlungur** ​is ‌therefore a ​scholarly ​transliteration rather ​than ​an attested ​ancient ‌spelling; it ​encodes ‌the reconstructed ​sound ‌of the ​name ‌for modern ​use, ‌and no ​mark ​in it ‌is ‌decorative.

‌Yurlungur is ​transmitted ​orally in ‌Yolŋu ​Matha and ​was ‌first recorded ​in ​English-based orthographies ‌by ​anthropologists in ‌the ​early twentieth ​century. ​There is ​no ‌single Indigenous ‌script ​corresponding to ‌the ​name; ​the forms ‌**Yurlungur**, ‌**Yulunggur**, **Julunggul**, ‌and ‌**Yurluŋgur** represent ​different ‌transcription conventions ​and ​clan pronunciations. ​The ‌PuniCodex restoration ​capitalizes ​the conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization as ​a ​proper noun. ​Because ‌the ASCII ​form ‌*yurlungur* already ​encodes ‌the ​same romanized ‌sequence ‌without distinctive ​diacritics ​or special ​letters, ​the name ‌is ‌a plain ​restoration.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Yurlungur** ​is the ‌great ‌copper python ​of ​the Yolŋu ​peoples ​of northeast ​Arnhem ‌Land — ​a ​Rainbow Serpent ‌whose swallowing ​of ‌the boy ​Wawi ‌at the ​first ​circumcision became ​the ​template for ​male ‌initiation across ​the ‌Murngin world. ​He ‌is not ​merely ‌a monster; ​he ‌is the ​law ​itself, the ‌waterhole guardian, ‌and ‌the ancestor ​who ​transforms boys ‌into ​men.[^1]

### Initiation

​Yurlungur ‌swallows the ​novice ​and releases ‌him ​as a ‌man; ​his waterhole ​is ​the first ​borum ‌ground.

### Rainbow ‌Serpent

​The copper ‌snake ​whose body ​arcs across ‌sky ‌and waterhole, ‌binding ‌rain, fertility, ​and ‌ancestral power.

### ​Guardian ​of Waterholes

​He ‌dwells in ​the ​deep sacred ​wells; ‌to disturb ​them ​is to ​risk ‌drought, flood, ​and ‌sickness.

### Ancestral ​Law

His ‌story ​encodes the ‌rules ‌of food ​taboo, ​kinship, and ​ritual ​obligation that ‌hold ‌Yolŋu society ​together.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Yurlungur ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the name:[^1]

- ‌**Copper ​python** ​— ​The ​living form ​of ‌Yurlungur ​himself; ‌the snake ​that ‌is ​both ‌ancestor ​and law
- ‌**Rainbow** ​— ​The ‌celestial trace ‌of ‌the ​serpent ​moving between ‌waterhole ​and ​sky; ‌sign ​of rain ​and ‌potency
- ​**Waterhole** ‌— The ​dwelling ​place ​of ​the ‌great snake ‌and ​the ‌portal ​through which ​novices ‌pass
- ‌**Bullroarer** ‌— The ‌sacred ​voice ‌of ​the ​serpent heard ​during ‌initiation; ​its ​sound must ​not ‌be ​heard ​by ​women or ‌uninitiated
- ​**White ‌ochre** ​— The ‌clay ​with ‌which ‌initiates and ​ritual ​objects ​are ​painted; ‌the mark ‌of ​transformation

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The central Yurlungur myth ​is an initiation narrative: a boy breaks a ‌food prohibition, is swallowed by the great copper ‌python, and is restored to his kin only ​after the correct ritual response. In that single ​event the whole logic of Yolŋu male initiation ​— death to childhood, passage through the ancestor's ​body, rebirth as a man — is enacted ​for the first time. The early ethnographies differ ‌in detail, even in the serpent's gender; the ​myths below follow the common structure.[^1]

### The Swallowing ​of Wawi (Murngin)

At the first borum ceremony, ‌the boy Wawi ate food that had been ​forbidden to him — and the great copper ‌python, sleeping in the deep waterhole, heard the ​law being broken. Yurlungur rose, traveled through the ‌earth to where the people were camped, and ​**swallowed the boy whole**. The ancestors were dismayed; ​the ceremony could not continue with the law's ​transgression unexpired. The boy's mother followed his tracks ​to the edge of the sacred pool, the ​place where the human world opens into the ‌ancestral realm, and there she wept and ​sang. Moved — or shamed — by her ‌grief, the python **vomited the boy out**, alive ​but no longer a child. From that day ‌the pattern was set: every novice must enter ​the ancestral body and emerge again. Initiation is, ‌in the myth's own terms, a controlled swallowing: ​the boy dies into the snake and is ‌reborn as a man.[^2]

### The Mother at the ​Waterhole (Murngin)

The mother's pursuit is as important ​as the snake's swallowing. She traces Wawi to ‌the rim of the sacred pool and there ‌does the one thing the law cannot do ‌without her: she **mourns correctly** — weeping, singing, ​calling the ancestor by the obligations it owes ​her line. The ethnographers who recorded the cycle ‌in the 1920s and 1930s (Warner, then the ​Berndts) heard in this scene the partnership of ​male and female knowledge in initiation: the men ‌own the rite, the bullroarer, and the enclosure, ​but the relational power that compels the ancestor ​to give the child back belongs to the ‌mother and her kin. The story thus ​encodes more than a punishment. It maps the ‌division of religious labor that holds Yolŋu society ​together — **the law swallows; the kinship system ​gives back** — and it makes the waterhole, ​where the two worlds touch, the most dangerous ​and most necessary place in the country.

### The ‌First Borum Ground (Murngin)

After Wawi's return, the ‌ground around Yurlungur's waterhole became the prototype of ​the borum ground — the cleared ceremonial space ‌where, in every generation since, novices are separated ​from women and children, painted with white ochre, ​shown the sacred objects of adulthood, and made ‌to hear the bullroarer's voice, which is the ‌serpent's own. The myth supplies the architecture: a ‌dangerous perimeter, an ancestral interior, a transformation that ‌cannot be undone. The novices who enter the ​enclosure are told, in the old men's instruction, ‌that they too have been inside the great ​snake; the pain and fear of the rite ​are the memory of its body. A borum ​is therefore not an imitation of the myth ‌but its **repetition** — the first swallowing ​carried forward, boy by boy, so that the ​ancestor's act at the beginning remains alive at ​every beginning since.

### Rainbow Serpent Typology (Comparative)

Yurlungur ‌belongs to the Rainbow Serpent family that stretches ​across Aboriginal Australia — **Ngalyod** in western Arnhem ​Land, the **Waugal** of the southwest, **Wanambi** in ​the central deserts, and dozens of locally owned ‌names beside. Like them he links water, fertility, ​and ancestral law; like them he punishes the ‌breaking of taboo and rewards the keeping of ​it with rain and children. But the comparative ‌label can mislead. 'Rainbow Serpent' is an English ​scholarly convenience, not an Aboriginal category, and the ‌regional figures differ sharply: Yurlungur is specifically tied ‌to male initiation and to the copper-coloured python ​that gives him his name, while Berndt's Kunapipi ​materials make the cognate serpent **Yulunggur a female ​mother-ancestor** of a different rite. The honest summary ​is that Australia does not have one rainbow ‌snake but hundreds of owned, local ancestors who ‌share a grammar — **water, law, danger, and ​the crossing between worlds**.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Yurlungur ​is best ‌understood ‌within the ​Yolŋu ​moieties (*Dhuwa* ​and ​*Yirritja*) and ​the ‌clan-specific song ​cycles ​(*manikay*) ‌that map ​his ‌journeys between ​waterholes. ‌He is ​not ​a universal ​Aboriginal ​god but ​a ‌regional ancestor ​whose ‌story is ​owned ‌and transmitted ​by ‌particular Yolŋu ​lineages. ‌Comparative anthropologists ​have ​grouped him ‌with ‌Rainbow ‌Serpent figures ​across ​the continent, ‌yet ​Yolŋu custodians ​emphasize ‌the local ​specificity ​of his ‌name, ​sites, and ‌ritual ​obligations; even ​the ​written sources ​disagree, ‌Warner's Murngin ‌python ​Julunggul being ‌male ​and ​Berndt's Kunapipi ‌snake ‌Yulunggur female. ‌In ‌modern discourse ​he ‌appears in ​Indigenous ​land-rights testimony, ​in ‌museum interpretations ​of ​Arnhem Land ​art, ‌and in ​scholarly ​discussions of ​Aboriginal ‌religion and ​environmental ‌knowledge.[^1]

Within ​the ‌Aboriginal ​tradition, closely ‌related ‌names in ​the ​corpus include ​[[altjira|Altjira]], ​[[baiame|Baiame]], [[bunjil|Bunjil]], ‌[[daramulum|Daramulum]], ‌[[eingana|Eingana]], and ​[[gnowee|Gnowee]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Yurlungur ​remains ‌a living ‌ancestor ​for ​Yolŋu ​peoples. His ​story ​is ‌performed ​in initiation, ​painted ‌in ​bark paintings ‌and ​on ‌bodies, ​and invoked ​in ​claims ​to ​country and ‌water. ​Anthropologists ‌from ​Warner and ‌the ​Berndts ‌onward ​have used ‌the ​Murngin ​material ‌as a ‌classic ‌case ​study in ​Australian ‌Aboriginal ​religion, ​kinship, and ‌ritual. ​In ​wider ‌Australian culture, ​the ‌Rainbow ​Serpent ​— including ​figures ​such ‌as ‌Yurlungur — ​has ‌become ​an emblem ​of ‌Indigenous ‌ecological ‌knowledge and ‌the ​deep ‌connection ​between sacred ​law ​and ‌the ​care of ​water. ​Contemporary ‌Yolŋu ​artists continue ​to ​depict ‌the ​great copper ‌python, ​and ‌his name ​is ‌cited ‌in ​discussions of ​cultural ​heritage, ​repatriation, ‌and Indigenous ‌intellectual ​property.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The ​material ‌evidence for ‌Yurlungur ​is ​held in ​Yolŋu ​ceremonial ​objects, rock ‌art, ​and ​sacred sites ‌rather ​than ‌in ​excavated strata. ‌Bark ​paintings ​from northeast ​Arnhem ​Land ​depict the ‌Rainbow ​Serpent ‌and the ​initiation ‌complex; ​notable ‌collections are ​held ‌by ​the Australian ​Institute ‌of ‌Aboriginal and ‌Torres ​Strait ​Islander Studies ‌(AIATSIS), ​the ​National ‌Museum of ​Australia, ​and ‌the Museum ​and ‌Art ​Gallery of ​the ​Northern ​Territory. ‌The waterholes ‌identified ​as ‌Yurlungur's dwelling ​remain ​active ‌sacred sites, ‌and ‌access ‌to them ​is ‌governed ​by ​Yolŋu customary ​law. ‌Archaeological ​research in ​the ​region ‌has documented ​long-term ​Aboriginal ​occupation of ‌the ​Arnhem ‌Land ​plateau and ‌adjacent ​coastal ‌plains, providing ‌the ​environmental ​context within ​which ​the ‌Yurlungur narratives ‌are ​embedded.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Yurlungur ​asks us ‌to think ‌about transformation ​as something ​that happens ​through the ​body of ​an ancestor ‌rather than ​through individual ​will. The ‌boy does ​not choose ‌to be ​swallowed; the ‌law chooses ​him. He ​does ​not engineer ​his own ​rebirth; his ‌mother's grief, ​the snake's ‌response, and ​the community's ‌ritual competence ​restore him. ‌Initiation is ​therefore not ‌a personal ​achievement but ​a social ‌event: the ‌whole kinship ‌system ​must hold ​for one ‌person to ​change.

In ​a world ‌that prizes ​autonomy, Yurlungur ​offers a ‌counter-image of ​becoming. To ‌become a ​man is ​to be ​eaten by ​the law, ‌to lose ‌the name ​one ‌had as ​a child, ​and to ‌be returned ‌with obligations ‌one did ‌not choose. ​The snake ‌is frightening ​not because ​he is ​cruel but ‌because he ​is impersonal: ​he enforces ​the taboo ‌whether ​the boy ​understands it ​or not. ‌Yet he ​is also ‌the guardian ​of water, ‌the bringer ​of rain, ‌and the ‌ancestor who ​makes the ​country habitable. ​His fierceness ​and his ‌generosity are ‌the same ​thing.[^1]
